## What the model says

The censored shifted Wald model ([Miller et al., 2018](https://doi.org/10.1177/0146621617710465)) is a
simplification of the diffusion model ([Ratcliff & McKoon,
2008](https://doi.org/10.1162/neco.2008.12-06-420)) for tasks with few errors. Evidence for the correct
response accumulates at rate `drift` with noise until it reaches `bound`; the time this takes follows a
Wald (inverse Gaussian) distribution, and the response time adds the non-decision time `ndt`. For a
response at decision time $t$ = rt − `ndt`, with $v$ = `drift`, $a$ = `bound` and the noise `s` fixed at 1, the
density is

$$
f(t) = \frac{a}{\sqrt{2\pi t^3}} \exp\left(-\frac{(a - v t)^2}{2t}\right).
$$

In the `simple` version there is no second boundary for errors. An error at time $t$ is a censored
observation: a trial on which the correct response had not been reached by $t$. It enters the likelihood
with the survival function $S(t) = 1 - F(t)$, where $F$ is the cumulative distribution of the Wald: the
probability that the accumulator is still on its way.
`bound` here is the distance from the start to the correct boundary, half the boundary separation of the
diffusion model (the distance between its two boundaries), and `drift` is positive. The competing-risks
version `crisk` gives each response its own accumulator. Both start at `zr` × `bound`, where `zr` is the
relative starting point between 0 and 1; one runs the distance (1 − `zr`) × `bound` to the upper
boundary with rate `drift`, the other the distance `zr` × `bound` to the lower boundary with rate
−`drift`, and the first to arrive gives the response. The likelihood of a response at $t$ is its own accumulator's Wald density times the other
accumulator's survival at $t$. In `crisk`, `bound` is the full boundary separation and `drift` can be
negative, as in the diffusion model.

## The task

One trial is a choice between two responses, with the response time recorded; bmm codes them 0 (lower)
and 1 (upper), and in this model 1 is usually the correct response. The task panel draws the
accumulation under the current parameters, with the noise held fixed while the sliders move. In
`simple` one accumulator rises from the start toward `bound`; an error has no boundary of its own and
stops the accumulator before it arrives. In `crisk` the two accumulators run at once, each in its own
lane: the upper one from the start up, the lower one from the start down. An accumulator that wanders
away from its boundary leaves its lane for a while, and the one that loses the race is drawn fainter.

## Explore

In `simple`, the blue curve is the density of a correct response at each response time and the orange
curve the likelihood of an error at that time, the probability that no correct response has come yet.
They share the axis, but one is a density and the other a probability. In `crisk` the two curves are
defective densities, upper responses above the axis and lower responses below, and each area is the
probability of that response. In `simple`, raising `drift` makes correct responses faster and less
variable: the decision time has mean $a/v$ and variance $a/v^3$. In `crisk`, raising `drift` moves area
from lower to upper responses, and moving it away from 0 in either direction makes the response it works
against faster and less variable. At drift 0 neither accumulator has a finite mean finishing time, so
both responses have long tails. The response `drift` favours changes differently: its median and
interquartile range first grow as `drift` leaves 0 and shrink only at larger drifts. Raising `bound`
makes responses slower and more spread out. `ndt` shifts everything. The time axis ends at 6 s at most.

Slider ranges come from bmm's default priors for `cswald()`. In `simple`, `drift` is estimated on the log
scale with a normal(0, 1) prior, `bound` on the log scale with normal(0, 0.3), and `ndt` on the log scale
with normal(−2, 0.3); each slider spans the prior mean ± 3 SD: `drift` from 0.05 to 20.1, `bound` from
0.41 to 2.46, `ndt` from 0.05 to 0.33 s. In `crisk`, `drift` has an identity link and a normal(0, 1)
prior, so it runs from −3 to 3; `bound` and `ndt` keep their ranges, and `zr` is estimated on the logit
scale with normal(0, 0.3), from 0.29 to 0.71. bmm fixes `zr` at 0.5 unless the formula estimates it. The
sliders start at the prior means (dashed). Switching the version restarts the parameters there, since
`drift` and `bound` mean different things in the two versions.

## Across task settings

The likelihood of `cswald()` has no task-setting variable. Conditions of an experiment enter only if the
bmm formula lets the parameters differ between them, as in `drift ~ 0 + condition`; what the model then
predicts in each condition follows from the estimated parameters.

What does change across tasks is how good the approximation is, and the panel *Compared with the
diffusion model* shows it. It draws this model's curves over the [diffusion model](ddm.qmd)'s with the
same parameters; for `simple`, the diffusion model gets twice `bound` as its boundary separation and
its start in the middle. Its readout gives the diffusion model's probability of a lower response, the
error rate the comparison is about. When the diffusion model
gives few lower responses, the correct-response densities nearly coincide. As errors become frequent,
they part: `simple` has no density for errors at all and keeps all its area on correct responses, while
the diffusion model moves area to the lower boundary. In `crisk` both models have both densities; they
come close when the readout's P(lower) is near 0 or 1 and differ most when it is near 0.5.
bmm's [cswald article](https://venpopov.com/bmm/articles/bmm_cswald.html) recommends `simple` for error rates
below 20% and `crisk` above.

## In bmm

```{=html}
<div class="ex-widget">
  <pre class="ex-code" id="cswald-code"></pre>
  <button type="button" class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary" id="cswald-copy">Copy</button>
</div>
<script type="module" src="../js/pages/cswald.js"></script>
```

The code updates with the controls. `cswald()` defines the model, `dcswald()` returns the log likelihood
of response times and responses, and `bmf()` writes the formula for `bmm()`, which estimates the
parameters from trial-level data; `my_data` stands for your own data, and fitting runs Stan through brms.
The comment under the `dcswald()` call holds the values this page computes for it. To compare `bound`
across versions or with `ddm()`, multiply the `simple` estimate by 2. See the
[cswald article](https://venpopov.com/bmm/articles/bmm_cswald.html) for the full model and the reference
pages for [`cswald()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/cswald.html) and
[`dcswald()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/cswald_dist.html).
